titulo: Cenário 1 — Customer Support Resolution Agent (banco de treino)

questoes.pergunta: Velora Logistics runs a customer support agent built with the Claude Agent SDK; it resolves returns, billing disputes, and account issues through MCP tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human), targeting 80%+ first-contact resolution. Last week, in 6% of tracking inquiries the agent told customers that no shipment exists for their order and closed the case. Re-running the same lookups an hour later found the shipment in almost every one of those cases, and the incidents cluster in windows when the carrier gateway's error dashboard shows spikes. What is the most likely root cause?
opcoes: lookup_order reports gateway failures in the same shape as a successful search with no matches, so the agent cannot tell an outage from an order that does not exist.
The system prompt does not tell the agent to retry lookup_order after an empty result, so it gives up after the first response instead of searching again.
lookup_order's description does not document the order-number format, so during incidents the agent passes malformed identifiers the backend cannot match.
The agent's context grows too long during busy periods, so it loses the order number from earlier turns and searches with a truncated identifier.
questoes.explicacao: Lookups that come back empty during gateway error spikes and succeed when repeated show that access failures are being reported as valid empty results. When an outage looks like 'no matches', the agent has no reason to retry or escalate and confidently tells the customer the order does not exist. Tools must distinguish access failures (with retry-relevant metadata) from successful queries that found nothing, so the agent can decide correctly.
feedbacks: Correct. A failure disguised as an empty result removes the signal the agent needs to choose between retrying, escalating, and answering 'not found'.

Tempting, because a retry would often succeed here. But retrying every empty result also wastes calls on orders that genuinely do not exist; the defect is that the tool does not say which kind of empty this is.
Plausible for misroutes in general, but the same identifiers succeed an hour later, which rules out a format problem and points to the upstream failure.
Context loss can corrupt identifiers in long sessions, but it would not line up with carrier gateway error spikes or disappear when the same lookup is simply repeated.

questoes.pergunta:
Velora Logistics' support agent (Claude Agent SDK; MCP tools get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human; target of 80%+ first-contact resolution) has a returns-only variant whose agentic loop an engineer wrote by hand:

for turn in range(12):
    resp = client.messages.create(model=MODEL, tools=TOOLS, messages=messages)
    messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": resp.content})
    text = " ".join(b.text for b in resp.content if b.type == "text")
    if "submitted" in text.lower() or "anything else" in text.lower():
        break
    messages.append({"role": "user", "content": run_tools(resp.content)})

In 4% of return conversations, no process_refund execution appears in the logs, although the last model response contained a process_refund tool_use block. These conversations ended after 3 or 4 iterations. What is the flaw?
opcoes: Tool results go back in a separate user-role message instead of inside the assistant's own turn, so the model cannot link each result to the call that produced it.
The 12-iteration cap is too low for multi-item returns, so complex conversations reach the limit before the refund step and then end without ever having run it.
The loop stops on phrases in the assistant's text, not on stop_reason, so a response saying "submitted" that also requests a tool exits before the tool runs.
The loop never checks for stop_reason "max_tokens", so a response cut off mid-generation is treated as complete and the refund step is skipped.
questoes.explicacao: The termination test inspects the assistant's text for phrases instead of stop_reason. When a response contains both text ('submitted') and a tool_use block, stop_reason is 'tool_use', but the phrase match exits before the tool runs. The loop should continue while stop_reason is 'tool_use' and end on 'end_turn'; natural-language signals, assistant text, and iteration caps are not reliable primary stopping mechanisms.
feedbacks: Returning tool results in a user-role message is the correct protocol, so this is not the flaw; results are linked to calls through their tool_use IDs.
A cap as the primary stop is an anti-pattern, but these conversations ended after 3–4 iterations, far below 12, so the cap is not what cut them short.
Correct. Phrase matching on text ignores stop_reason; a response can say 'submitted' and still be waiting for its tool call to run.
Handling max_tokens matters, but the failing responses contained a complete process_refund tool_use block, so truncation does not explain the skipped call.

questoes.pergunta: Velora Logistics runs a customer support agent built with the Claude Agent SDK; it resolves returns, billing disputes, and account issues through MCP tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human), targeting 80%+ first-contact resolution. For "marked delivered but not received" claims the agent is inconsistent: on near-identical cases it sometimes issues a refund at once, sometimes calls lookup_order to check the proof-of-delivery photo, and sometimes escalates. The system prompt already has 10 few-shot examples, each a clear-cut request (a damaged parcel, a wrong address) followed only by the final tool call. Which statement about this behavior is correct?
opcoes: The example set is too small; adding 20–30 more clear-cut examples (damaged parcels, wrong addresses, late deliveries) will cover enough variations for the model to match these claims.
Few-shot examples cannot steer tool selection; a choice like this needs a routing rule that maps each request category, such as delivered-not-received, to one fixed tool.
The inconsistency is ordinary run-to-run variation; running each claim twice and keeping the action both runs agree on would make the decision deterministic without prompt changes.
The examples show only easy cases and final actions; 2–4 examples of this ambiguous case that explain why one action beat the alternatives would give the model a basis.
questoes.explicacao: The existing examples demonstrate only easy cases with no reasoning, so the model has no guidance for the case that is actually ambiguous. Two to four targeted few-shot examples for this scenario, showing why one action was chosen over the plausible alternatives, let the model generalize the judgment instead of matching surface patterns.
feedbacks: More examples of easy cases add tokens without teaching the judgment the ambiguous case needs; volume is not the gap.
Few-shot examples are an effective way to show tool selection for ambiguous requests; a fixed routing rule would also ignore the evidence (proof photo, history) that should drive the choice.
Voting between runs can hide variance but gives the model no decision rule; two runs can agree on the wrong action.
Correct. Targeted examples that show the reasoning (check proof of delivery before refunding, escalate when evidence conflicts) let the model handle similar ambiguous claims.

questoes.pergunta: Velora Logistics runs a customer support agent built with the Claude Agent SDK; it resolves returns, billing disputes, and account issues through MCP tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human), targeting 80%+ first-contact resolution. Today a programmatic gate blocks process_refund until get_customer returns a verified customer ID. A product manager proposes removing the gate because, in a 2,000-conversation test with a strengthened system prompt ("You MUST verify identity before any refund"), the agent verified first in 99.6% of refund cases, and the gate is extra code to maintain. How should you evaluate this proposal?
opcoes: Keep the gate: 99.6% still means about 8 unverified refunds per 2,000 conversations, and only enforcement in the call path removes that failure rate for a financial operation.
Accept the proposal if a larger test of 20,000 conversations confirms compliance above 99.5%, since that sample size would show the prompt is reliable enough to depend on in production.
Accept the proposal and add few-shot examples of verification before refunds to the prompt, which closes the small gap the instruction alone still leaves.
Replace the gate with a programmatic nightly audit that reverses refunds issued without verification, reaching the same outcome with less code in the request path.
questoes.explicacao: When compliance must be deterministic, as with identity verification before refunds, prompt instructions alone keep a non-zero failure rate, even at 99.6%. A programmatic prerequisite blocks the downstream call until the verified ID exists, so the failure cannot occur. The cost of maintaining a small gate is far lower than the cost of unverified refunds.
feedbacks: Correct. Financial operations that require verification need deterministic enforcement; a prompt has a non-zero failure rate however strongly it is worded.
A larger sample measures the failure rate more precisely but does not remove it; the requirement is that unverified refunds never execute, not that they are rare.
Few-shot examples improve compliance probabilistically, which still leaves a non-zero failure rate for money leaving the company.
A nightly audit acts after the money is gone and depends on reversals succeeding; a preventive gate stops the call before it happens.

questoes.pergunta: Velora Logistics' support agent (Claude Agent SDK; MCP tools get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human; target of 80%+ first-contact resolution) resolves only 64% of cases on first contact. Its system prompt says only: "Escalate when a case is complex or the customer seems unhappy." Transcripts show two near-identical claims for a parcel left at the wrong address: one was reshipped by the agent, the other escalated after the customer typed in capital letters. Meanwhile, a request to waive a customs-duty charge, which policy does not cover, was handled with no human involved. The team has two weeks and no labeled ticket history. What is the most effective fix?
opcoes: Escalate every claim above $250 and let the agent resolve everything below that amount, so the decision is deterministic instead of depending on the model's judgment.
Add a sentiment check that escalates as soon as the customer's messages turn negative, since an unhappy customer is already one of the triggers the prompt states.
Escalate whenever the agent needs more than three tool calls on a case, using the number of calls as a measurable proxy for complexity.
Replace the vague rule with explicit escalation criteria (policy gaps, requests for a human, no progress) and few-shot examples of escalate versus resolve.
questoes.explicacao: 'Complex or unhappy' gives the agent no usable boundary, so similar cases diverge and a policy gap goes unescalated. Explicit escalation criteria (policy exceptions or gaps, explicit human requests, inability to progress) with few-shot examples of escalate versus resolve fix the decision boundary directly. It fits the two-week constraint and needs no labeled data or new infrastructure.
feedbacks: A fixed amount is deterministic, but amount does not measure what needs a human: the customs waiver may be small and still outside policy, while a large misdelivery is routine.
Sentiment is an unreliable proxy for complexity; it is what escalated the routine reshipment typed in capital letters.
Tool-call count reflects investigation work, not whether policy allows the agent to act; a policy-gap request can need one call and a routine case several.
Correct. Unclear decision boundaries are the root cause; explicit criteria with contrasting examples are the proportionate first fix.

questoes.pergunta: Velora Logistics runs a customer support agent built with the Claude Agent SDK; it resolves returns, billing disputes, and account issues through MCP tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human), targeting 80%+ first-contact resolution. Freight customers often raise several shipments in one conversation. Each lookup_order result has about 60 fields, including every hub scan and GPS ping, while support decisions use about six of them. By the tenth turn of a three-shipment dispute the context exceeds 45k tokens, and the agent starts to overlook the delivery window the customer stated at the start. What is the most effective first step?
opcoes: Move the agent to a model with a larger context window, so that multi-shipment conversations stay well below the limit even as their lookup results keep accumulating.
Trim each lookup_order result to the fields support decisions use (status, promised and delivered dates, charges, return eligibility) before it enters context.
Summarize the conversation every five turns, so that earlier lookup_order results are compressed into short notes together with the dialogue.
Add a system-prompt instruction telling the agent to ignore scan and GPS fields when it reasons about a claim, so it focuses on relevant ones.
questoes.explicacao: Tool results accumulate in context and consume tokens out of proportion to their relevance: here about 90% of each lookup is noise for the decision. Trimming verbose tool output to the relevant fields before it accumulates keeps the context small and the customer's early statements in focus.
feedbacks: A larger window postpones the limit but keeps the irrelevant tokens in context, and attention to the customer's early statements still degrades.
Correct. Trimming at the source keeps only the fields the decisions need, so lookups stop crowding out the conversation.
Progressive summarization risks condensing exactly the dates and amounts the agent needs into vague notes, and verbose results still pile up between summaries.
The instruction does not remove the tokens; the irrelevant fields still fill the context and dilute attention.

questoes.pergunta: Velora Logistics' support agent (Claude Agent SDK; MCP tools get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human; target of 80%+ first-contact resolution) handles billing disputes that can run for days, and older turns are summarized because long disputes exceeded the context budget. After a summarization, the agent quoted a disputed surcharge as "about $40" instead of $43.80 and mixed up which of two invoices was contested. Design 1: instruct the summarizer to keep all numbers, dates, and invoice IDs verbatim. Design 2: extract invoice numbers, amounts, dates, and statuses into a case-facts block, updated after each tool call and included in every prompt outside the summarized history. Which assessment is correct?
opcoes: Design 2, because facts kept outside the summarized history never pass through compression, so no later summary can round, merge, or drop them.
Design 1, because it protects the same facts with no extra state to maintain, and the summarizer already sees each number it has to keep.
Neither is needed: drop summarization and send the complete conversation history in every request, so that no transactional fact is ever compressed.
Design 2 works only if the case-facts block sits in the middle of the prompt, between the summary and the latest turns, where the model weighs it most.
questoes.explicacao: Progressive summarization tends to condense amounts, dates, and identifiers into vague text. Keeping transactional facts in a persistent case-facts block, included in each prompt outside the summarized history, protects them from every compression round, whereas an instruction to the summarizer is still probabilistic.
feedbacks: Correct. Facts held outside the summarized history cannot be rounded or merged by summarization; the instruction-only design can still slip.
Instructions to the summarizer help but remain probabilistic; the rounding of $43.80 to 'about $40' is exactly the progressive-summarization risk.
Complete history matters for coherence, but summarization exists here because long disputes exceeded the context budget; removing it brings that problem back.
The middle of a long input is where information is most often missed (lost in the middle); key facts belong in a clearly marked block, not buried mid-prompt.

questoes.pergunta: Velora Logistics runs a customer support agent built with the Claude Agent SDK; it resolves returns, billing disputes, and account issues through MCP tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human), targeting 80%+ first-contact resolution. When it reviews a customer's invoices, the agent also flags suspected billing errors for the billing team, which reports that 55% of flags are false alarms. After "Only flag an invoice when you are highly confident it is wrong" was added to the prompt, the false-alarm rate moved only to 51%. The billing team needs at least 80% of flags to be real errors. What should you change?
opcoes: Raise the bar further: "Flag only when you are at least 95% confident; when in doubt, do not flag," so borderline invoices stop reaching the team.
Have the agent attach a confidence score to each flag and forward only flags scored above 0.8, so the team receives only the most certain cases.
Define what to flag (a surcharge with no matching service event, a duplicated charge) and what to skip (differences the published tariff explains).
Add context: "Be conservative; the billing team is small and false alarms cost them hours," so the model understands why precision matters.
questoes.explicacao: General instructions such as 'only flag when highly confident' or 'be conservative' barely change precision, as the 55%→51% result shows. Specific categorical criteria that say which discrepancies to report and which to skip give the model a concrete test to apply to each invoice.
feedbacks: A stronger confidence threshold is still a vague instruction; the previous attempt already showed this kind of wording barely moves precision.
Filtering by self-reported confidence replaces criteria with the model's own uncertainty; it never tells the model what counts as a billing error.
Correct. Categorical criteria for what to report versus skip improve precision where confidence or caution instructions do not.
Explaining the cost is useful context, but 'be conservative' is the kind of general instruction that fails to improve precision.

questoes.pergunta: Velora Logistics runs a customer support agent built with the Claude Agent SDK; it resolves returns, billing disputes, and account issues through MCP tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human), targeting 80%+ first-contact resolution. Compliance now requires that process_refund never runs unless get_customer has returned a verified customer ID in the session and lookup_order has confirmed that the order belongs to that customer. Last month, 9 refunds were issued against orders of a different customer with the same surname. Which TWO implementation choices meet this requirement? Choose TWO.
opcoes: Add a hook that intercepts process_refund calls and blocks them unless session state holds a verified ID from get_customer.
Have process_refund check on the server that the order's owner matches the session's verified ID, and return an error otherwise.
Add few-shot examples that show get_customer, then lookup_order, then process_refund in typical refund conversations.
Add an explicit rule to the system prompt, written in capitals, stating that refunds require a verified identity and a confirmed owner.
Add a PostToolUse hook that logs the customer ID of every refund, so that mismatches show up in a daily compliance report.
questoes.explicacao: The requirement is a hard prerequisite on a financial operation, so it needs enforcement in the call path. Intercepting process_refund until a verified ID exists, and checking order ownership on the server, both make the wrong refund impossible rather than unlikely. Prompt rules, examples, and after-the-fact logging leave a non-zero failure rate.
feedbacks: Correct. A programmatic prerequisite blocks the refund until verification has completed, which a prompt cannot guarantee.
Correct. A server-side ownership check is a deterministic gate: the refund cannot execute against an order that belongs to someone else.
Few-shot examples improve the usual ordering but do not block the cases where the model deviates, which is where the 9 bad refunds came from.
Capitals and stronger wording still rely on probabilistic compliance; the requirement is that the call never runs without verification.
This hook only records what happened; the refunds would still be issued and discovered later, so it detects rather than prevents.

questoes.pergunta: Velora Logistics' support agent (Claude Agent SDK; MCP tools get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human; target of 80%+ first-contact resolution) handles tracking questions, address changes, billing disputes, and returns, often several in one conversation. An architect proposes replacing the agent's model-driven tool selection with a fixed decision tree: always get_customer, then lookup_order, then process_refund if eligible, otherwise escalate_to_human. Which TWO statements about this proposal are correct? Choose TWO.
opcoes: A fixed tree covers only the paths its authors anticipated, so a return that becomes a billing dispute falls outside it, while the model adapts.
With model-driven selection, Claude picks the next tool from what earlier results revealed, such as skipping lookup_order for an email change.
Model-driven selection requires tool_choice set to "any"; with "auto", the model cannot decide on its own which tool to call next.
Model-driven selection makes prerequisite gates unnecessary, because the model reasons about which tool has to come first before it calls anything.
The fixed tree behaves like the model-driven loop as long as each tool result is appended to the conversation history before the next step runs.
questoes.explicacao: In model-driven decision-making, Claude reasons over the context and prior tool results to decide which tool to call next, so it adapts when a request changes or needs fewer steps. A pre-configured tree runs the same sequence whatever the results show. Critical ordering such as verification before refunds is still enforced programmatically; that complements model-driven selection rather than replacing it.
feedbacks: Correct. Pre-configured trees are rigid; multi-concern conversations that change direction are where model-driven decisions pay off.
Correct. In the agentic loop, the model decides the next tool (or none) from the context and earlier results.
With "auto" the model decides whether and which tool to call; "any" only forces some tool call and is not what enables model-driven selection.
Model-driven choices are probabilistic; critical ordering such as verification before refunds still needs a programmatic gate.
Appending results lets the model reason, but a fixed tree ignores that reasoning: the sequence is set in advance whatever the results show.

questoes.pergunta: Velora Logistics runs a customer support agent built with the Claude Agent SDK; it resolves returns, billing disputes, and account issues through MCP tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human), targeting 80%+ first-contact resolution. The agent delegates shipment investigations to a subagent that queries three carrier tracking APIs. One carrier API returns HTTP 503 on about 7% of calls, and nearly all of those succeed on a second attempt. Today the subagent returns each 503 to the main agent at once; the main agent then re-delegates the whole investigation, adding about 40 seconds, and sometimes tells the customer that tracking is unavailable. Which statement about this behavior is correct?
opcoes: The design is right as it stands: the main agent owns the conversation, so it should make the retry decision for every call the subagent makes.
The subagent should drop the failing carrier and return the other two carriers' results as a complete answer, since partial data beats an error.
The fix belongs in the main agent's prompt: telling it to wait and re-delegate only once would remove most of the added latency.
The subagent should retry the 503 locally and pass up only failures it cannot resolve, along with the results it did get and what it attempted.
questoes.explicacao: Transient failures such as an intermittent 503 are best recovered where they occur. The subagent should retry locally and propagate to the main agent only errors it cannot resolve, together with partial results and what was attempted, so the main agent can decide without repeating the whole investigation.
feedbacks: Centralizing every retry makes the main agent handle routine noise and repeat whole investigations; transient failures belong to local recovery.
Returning partial data as a complete answer silently suppresses the failure; the main agent would not know one carrier's data is missing.
Tuning the re-delegation treats the symptom; the failure is still propagated before any local recovery has been tried.
Correct. Local recovery for transient failures, escalating only unresolved errors with partial results and attempts, removes the extra round trips.

questoes.pergunta: Velora Logistics runs a customer support agent built with the Claude Agent SDK; it resolves returns, billing disputes, and account issues through MCP tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human), targeting 80%+ first-contact resolution. Policy says refunds above $500 need a human. The rule lives only in the system prompt, and an audit found 11 refunds between $520 and $1,900 last month. An engineer proposes an Agent SDK hook that intercepts outgoing process_refund calls, blocks any above $500, and returns a message telling the agent to hand the case to escalate_to_human with the case details. How should you evaluate this proposal?
opcoes: Reject it: restating the $500 limit in the system prompt with examples of escalated refunds gets the same guarantee without adding code to the agent.
Adopt it, but let the hook lower the refund to $500 and allow the call through, so the customer is paid at once and a human reviews the rest.
Adopt it: intercepting the call guarantees no refund above $500 executes, and the redirect to escalate_to_human keeps the case moving.
Adopt it as monitoring only: let the calls through, log each violation, and alert a supervisor who can reverse the refund within the hour.
questoes.explicacao: A business rule that must always hold should be enforced by a hook that intercepts the outgoing tool call, not by prompt text that the audit already shows failing. Blocking the call and redirecting to escalate_to_human gives a deterministic guarantee and an alternative workflow, so the customer's case still moves forward.
feedbacks: The audit already shows the prompt-only rule failing 11 times a month; more prompt text keeps compliance probabilistic.
Issuing a partial refund automatically is itself a decision the policy reserves for a human above $500.
Correct. A tool call interception hook enforces the rule deterministically and redirects to the alternative workflow, human escalation.
Logging and later reversal is detective, not preventive; the money still goes out and the customer experience suffers when it is clawed back.

questoes.pergunta: Velora Logistics' support agent (Claude Agent SDK; MCP tools get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human; target of 80%+ first-contact resolution) also uses a generic MCP tool, manage_shipment(action, params), where action is "reroute", "hold", "update_contact", or "claim_damage" and params is a free-form object. In 14% of calls the agent sends params that belong to a different action, such as an address object for a hold. The MCP server team can change tool definitions this sprint but cannot change the backend services behind them. What is the most effective fix?
opcoes: Expand manage_shipment's description to list every action with its required params and two example calls, so the agent sees each combination.
When manage_shipment returns a validation error, have the agent call it again with the error message appended, so it corrects the params.
Add a classifier that selects the action value before each call, so the agent only has to fill in params for an action already chosen.
Split manage_shipment into reroute_shipment, hold_shipment, update_delivery_contact, and file_damage_claim, each with its own typed input schema.
questoes.explicacao: A generic tool with a free-form params object has no contract tying each action to its inputs, so mismatched parameters remain easy to send. Splitting it into purpose-specific tools with defined input and output contracts makes each action's parameters explicit, and the new tools can wrap the same backend services, which meets the constraint.
feedbacks: A richer description helps, but one tool with free-form params still has no contract per action, so the mismatch stays possible.
Retry with error feedback recovers some calls after the fact, but the generic interface keeps inviting wrong params on every call.
A separate classifier adds infrastructure to compensate for a tool that should not be generic in the first place.
Correct. Purpose-specific tools with typed schemas make parameters explicit, and they can call the same backend services.

questoes.pergunta: Velora Logistics runs a customer support agent built with the Claude Agent SDK; it resolves returns, billing disputes, and account issues through MCP tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human), targeting 80%+ first-contact resolution. Every lookup_order result includes the recipient's full phone number and address. Regulation requires that these details never reach a caller who is not the verified account holder. The system prompt says "Do not disclose recipient contact details to unverified callers," yet in a red-team test the agent revealed them in 3 of 200 attempts. What is the most effective first step?
opcoes: Add few-shot examples of the agent declining to share recipient contact details with unverified callers, including attempts that use social pressure.
Repeat the instruction at the start and end of the system prompt and in lookup_order's description, so it stays salient in long conversations.
Add a PostToolUse hook that masks contact fields in lookup_order results unless the session holds a verified ID, so the model never sees them.
Add an independent reviewer model that checks each outgoing reply for contact details and rewrites the reply before it reaches the caller.
questoes.explicacao: Prompt instructions give probabilistic compliance, and 3 of 200 is the residual failure they leave. A hook gives a deterministic guarantee: if a PostToolUse hook masks the fields for unverified sessions, the data never enters the model's context and cannot be disclosed.
feedbacks: Examples raise compliance but keep it probabilistic; a residual failure like 3 of 200 is what prompts cannot eliminate.
Placement and repetition improve salience, not guarantees; the data is still in context and can still leak.
Correct. Keeping the data out of the context for unverified callers turns a probabilistic rule into a guaranteed one.
A second model is itself probabilistic and adds latency and cost; the deterministic fix is to keep the data out of the context.

questoes.pergunta: Velora Logistics' support agent (Claude Agent SDK; MCP tools get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human; target of 80%+ first-contact resolution) also has a track_parcel tool for carrier tracking numbers, yet it often passes those numbers to lookup_order, which accepts only Velora order numbers, and then tells customers the order was not found. Two descriptions for lookup_order are proposed. Draft 1: "Looks up an order by its ID." Draft 2 adds the accepted format (VL- followed by 8 digits), example requests, the edge case that carrier tracking numbers belong to track_parcel, and that orders older than 18 months are archived. Which choice is best?
opcoes: Draft 2, because the accepted format, example requests, and when track_parcel applies give the model the boundary between the two tools that it lacks.
Draft 1, because short descriptions cost fewer tokens on every request, and the model can learn the ID format from the not-found results.
Draft 2, but with the edge cases moved into the system prompt, since the model ranks system-prompt instructions above tool descriptions.
Neither; add input validation that rejects malformed IDs in lookup_order, since a validation error teaches the model the format on retry.
questoes.explicacao: Tool descriptions are the primary mechanism the model uses to select tools. Including input formats, example queries, edge cases, and an explicit boundary with the similar tool (track_parcel) gives the model what it needs to route tracking numbers correctly.
feedbacks: Correct. Input formats, examples, edge cases, and boundaries in the description are what prevent this misrouting.
Learning from not-found results is exactly what is failing: the agent reads them as genuine misses and tells customers so.
The boundary belongs in the description of the tool being chosen; moving it away weakens selection rather than strengthening it.
Validation helps after a wrong call, but a format error does not tell the model that track_parcel is the right tool.

questoes.pergunta: Velora Logistics runs a customer support agent built with the Claude Agent SDK; it resolves returns, billing disputes, and account issues through MCP tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human), targeting 80%+ first-contact resolution. Customers reach the agent through a web chat where they are already logged in, so their customer ID is known when the session opens. The team wants every session to start with a get_customer call so the agent has account context before it chooses other tools. With tool_choice set to "auto", 18% of first turns are a text greeting or a lookup_order call instead. What should you change?
opcoes: Set tool_choice to {"type": "tool", "name": "get_customer"} on the first request only, then go back to "auto".
Set tool_choice to "any" for the whole conversation, so the model must call a tool on every turn instead of answering with plain text.
Keep tool_choice at "auto" and add an explicit system-prompt rule: "Your first action in every session must be a get_customer call."
Force {"type": "tool", "name": "get_customer"} on every turn, so account context is refreshed before any other tool is used.
questoes.explicacao: Forced tool selection guarantees that a specific tool is called first. Applying it only to the first request and returning to "auto" afterwards lets the agent process the following steps in later turns, choosing lookup_order, process_refund, or a text reply as needed.
feedbacks: Correct. Force the first call, then let the model choose the next steps in follow-up turns.
"any" guarantees some tool call, not get_customer specifically, and requiring a tool on every turn prevents normal replies to the customer.
A prompt rule is probabilistic; the 18% miss rate is what instructions alone produce.
Forcing the same tool on every turn would loop on get_customer and block other tools and replies; forcing belongs on the first step only.

questoes.pergunta: Velora Logistics' support agent (Claude Agent SDK; MCP tools get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human; target of 80%+ first-contact resolution) is reviewed after a rise in abandoned chats. When customers write "I want to talk to a person" or "agent please", the agent first calls get_customer and lookup_order and proposes a solution; 38% of those customers abandon the chat. The system prompt says: "Always try to resolve the issue before escalating. Escalate only if you cannot resolve it." What is the most likely root cause?
opcoes: escalate_to_human has a vague one-line description, so the agent does not recognize that the tool applies when a customer explicitly asks for a person.
The prompt applies "resolve first" to explicit requests for a human too; those should be honored at once, unlike frustrated customers who did not ask.
The agent has no sentiment detection, so it does not notice how frustrated these customers are and keeps investigating instead of escalating.
The agent's confidence in resolving these cases is too high, so it overestimates its ability to help and delays the escalation it should make.
questoes.explicacao: An explicit request for a human is an immediate escalation trigger and should be honored without first investigating. Offering to resolve fits a different case: a frustrated customer with a straightforward issue who has not asked for a person. The prompt collapses both into 'resolve first'.
feedbacks: A vague description can cause misrouting, but the prompt explicitly tells the agent to try resolving first, which explains the behavior directly.
Correct. Explicit requests for a human are honored immediately; offering to resolve is for straightforward issues where no person was requested.
Sentiment is an unreliable escalation proxy, and these customers stated their preference outright, so no inference about frustration is needed.
Self-reported confidence is not a reliable proxy, and the agent is following its instructions rather than overestimating itself.

questoes.pergunta: Velora Logistics runs a customer support agent built with the Claude Agent SDK; it resolves returns, billing disputes, and account issues through MCP tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human), targeting 80%+ first-contact resolution. The agent delegates policy questions to a subagent that searches the claims-policy library and returns its findings as one prose paragraph, such as "Late deliveries qualify for a refund within 30 days, and storage fees are waived on first occurrence...". The main agent quotes these findings to customers and in escalation handoffs. Reviewers cannot tell which document or section each statement came from, and twice the agent quoted a rule from the superseded 2023 policy as current. What is the flaw in this design?
opcoes: The subagent searches too many documents; limiting it to the single most relevant policy document per question would prevent conflicting statements.
The subagent merges findings into prose, dropping each statement's document, section, and effective date instead of returning them as fields.
The main agent does not reread the policy documents before quoting them, so it relies on the subagent's interpretation instead of the original text.
The subagent's prompt does not ask for customer-ready wording, so the main agent rewrites the text before sending it and loses details on the way.
questoes.explicacao: When findings pass between agents as merged prose, the metadata that supports attribution (document name, section, effective date) is lost. Structured outputs that keep each excerpt separate from its source metadata let the main agent cite the right document and notice superseded rules.
feedbacks: Narrowing the search may hide relevant rules and still returns unattributed prose; the defect is how findings are passed, not how many documents are searched.
Correct. Separating content from metadata in a structured format preserves attribution across the handoff.
Rereading everything in the main agent defeats the purpose of delegation and fills its context; attribution should travel with the findings.
Tone is a different concern; the defect is that each statement's source is discarded before it reaches the main agent.

questoes.pergunta: Velora Logistics' support agent (Claude Agent SDK; MCP tools get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human; target of 80%+ first-contact resolution) receives {"isError": true, "content": "Refund failed"} from process_refund for every failure. Logs show the agent retrying 3 to 5 times on refunds rejected because the 60-day claim window has expired, while giving up after one attempt when the payment gateway timed out. Which TWO changes to the error responses address this? Choose TWO.
opcoes: Return policy rejections as successful results with a "denied" status, so the agent stops treating them as failures.
Add an errorCategory to each error, such as "transient" for gateway timeouts and "business" for an expired claim window.
Add an isRetryable boolean, false for policy rejections, plus a customer-friendly explanation the agent can relay.
Return the same error for every failure and let the agent's loop apply exponential backoff to any failed call, up to five times.
Include the backend's raw exception message and stack trace in the error content, so the agent sees the underlying cause.
questoes.explicacao: A uniform error forces the agent to guess, so it retries rejections that can never succeed and abandons failures that would. Structured metadata (errorCategory plus an isRetryable flag, with a customer-friendly explanation for business rules) tells the agent which errors are worth retrying and what to say to the customer.
feedbacks: Disguising a rejection as a success removes the failure signal; the agent may report the refund as done or try other paths blindly.
Correct. A category lets the agent choose the recovery: retry transient failures, explain business rejections.
Correct. An explicit retryable flag prevents wasted retries, and the explanation lets the agent tell the customer why the refund cannot proceed.
Blind backoff wastes attempts on errors that can never succeed, such as an expired claim window, and still treats both cases alike.
Raw exceptions are unstructured and may expose internals; the agent still has to guess whether a retry can help.

questoes.pergunta: Velora Logistics' engineers build the MCP server behind their Claude Agent SDK support agent (tools get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human) and test it from Claude Code through a project-level .mcp.json committed to the repository, so every engineer gets the same server configuration. To speed up onboarding, a developer proposes putting the staging API key directly in the server's env block in .mcp.json, since the repository is private. How should you evaluate this proposal?
opcoes: Accept it: the repository is private and access-controlled, so a staging key in the committed .mcp.json adds no meaningful exposure for the team.
Reject it: keep the server in the committed .mcp.json but reference the key as ${VELORA_STAGING_KEY}, set in each engineer's environment.
Reject it: move the whole server definition into each engineer's ~/.claude.json, so the key stays on individual machines and out of the repository.
Accept it with a .gitignore entry for .mcp.json, so the file that contains the key never reaches the remote repository.
questoes.explicacao: Environment variable expansion in .mcp.json keeps the shared server configuration in version control while each engineer supplies the credential locally. That gives the team one versioned configuration without committing a secret.
feedbacks: Private repositories are still cloned, forked, and backed up widely; committing secrets is exactly what variable expansion avoids.
Correct. ${VAR} expansion in the project .mcp.json shares the configuration without sharing the secret.
User-level ~/.claude.json is for personal or experimental servers; moving shared team tooling there loses the single versioned configuration.
Ignoring .mcp.json means it is no longer shared, which defeats the reason for a project-level file.
